# The Heat Is Uneven: How Cities Can Make Summer Bearable

Summer heat has always been uncomfortable, but climate change has transformed seasonal discomfort into a public health crisis. Cities amplify this problem through the urban heat island effect: asphalt, concrete, and dark rooftops absorb solar radiation all day and release it slowly at night, keeping urban cores several degrees hotter than surrounding countryside. In the 1995 Chicago heat wave, more than 700 people died, most of them elderly residents of neighborhoods where temperatures peaked highest and social connections were weakest. More recently, Phoenix has recorded temperatures above 110 degrees Fahrenheit for weeks at a stretch, and European cities long built for temperate climates—Paris, Seville, Athens—have suffered deadly heat waves that their infrastructure was never designed to handle. The question facing urban planners is not whether to adapt but how, and the answer requires attention to trees, street design, housing, and transit, along with honest acknowledgment of the tradeoffs involved.
